body_markdown:
I frequently employ the writer’s “Wait, what?” trap about 500 words into a piece, having first made some sort of rational-sounding setup only to then adroitly drop the fact that I’ve done something unexpected or profoundly stupid with a degree of aplomb that makes the reader do the Scooby Doo-like jowels-flapping head shake. Here, reader, there will be no surprise, because I’ve already let the cat out of the bag with both the title and the lead photo. But humor me.


Me (actual): “I looked at a 2010 Toyota Camry six-speed manual.”


You (implied): “Wait, what?”


And with that little piece of wordsmithery out of the way, on with our story…


A number of things lead up to this questionable way to spend a Saturday morning, but it mainly had to do with the fact that, with 220,000 miles on it, the life of my 2003 BMW E39 530i is finite, and Maire Anne’s 90,000-mile 2013 Honda Fit has had a few surprising issues. Because there is no universe in which we are ever going to go out and buy a new car, I like to always have a bead on what I think I’d jump on in the used market if I had to produce a value-priced replacement car out of thin air in a few days. As much as I love BMWs, they’re hardly the cornerstone for reliability or economy as the mileage clicks up. (In fairness, everything requires service, and it’s not cheap on any car. But while our Honda has done some odd things, I do believe that many folks are truthful when they say “I owned that Honda/Toyota, drove it 150,000 miles, and it needed nothing but oil changes and brake jobs,” whereas if anyone says that about a BMW, I’d need to see them injected with sodium pentothal and strapped to a polygraph before I’d believe them.)


So I took some time and pounded on listing sites to see what I might unearth. I was on Craigslist (a shadow of its former self since Facebook Marketplace ate its lunch) and did a search for manual-transmission cars with under 150,000 miles for less than five grand, and a short ad for a 2010 Camry LE four-cylinder six-speed manual (say it with me: “Wait, what?”) came up. It said the car had 132,000 miles, ran well but had a loud exhaust and was throwing an oxygen sensor code, and was being sold because the owner worked in construction and had bought a truck. The asking price was $4200 or best offer. The photo of the potato-shaped white car with black steel wheels looked like reliable transportation for a galactic stormtrooper, but hey, I was trying to be open-minded.


Yeah… but six-speed, right?


Craigslist


Now, I have respect for Toyota but little love for their passenger cars, at least their sedans. I’ve always thought that the difference between Honda and Toyota is that Honda builds cars for people who actually enjoy driving, whereas Toyotas are built for people who merely tolerate it. My daughter inherited what was my mother’s 2007 Corolla, and while I’m glad that it soldiers on and costs her next to nothing to operate, I’d sooner eat damp lint than daily-drive it. But my 100-year-old neighbor Jeanette’s 2014 Honda Accord? Bring it on.


Still, not *everything* I drive needs to be interesting, right? And maybe, with a six-speed stick, a 16-year-old Camry would be interesting enough, right? It would be very different from anything else I’ve spent $4200 on, but maybe a boring reliable stick was what I needed.


It indeed was a stick.


Craigslist


I did some research and learned that the “Camry reliability” issue isn’t a total slam-dunk: The four-cylinder 2.4-liter 2AZ-FE engine that was in the Camry from 2002 through 2009 had oil-burning issues that resulted in a 10-year warranty extension and replacement of the rings and pistons. However, beginning in 2010, the 2.4 was replaced by the 169-horsepower 2.5-liter 2AR-FE that did not have this problem. Regarding the six-speed, apparently 2011 was the last year the Camry was available with a stick, and while production numbers aren’t available, the take rate for the manual is estimated at well under 1%. I did a search on Cars.com, and it found no 2010–11 Camry six-speeds. (To be clear, it “found” 10, but the photos of all 10 showed an automatic gearshift lever.) Because the rear fold-down seats in my E39 are so useful, I checked to make sure that the Camry has them, and the LE model does. However, the SE (“sport”) model doesn’t, as it has a brace behind the seats to stiffen the body. Curious about the SE and its “sport-tuned suspension,” I drilled into it and learned that the six-speed manual is only available with the four-cylinder, and if you want the much-quicker 268-hp 3.5-liter V-6, you have to take the automatic, which is a bizarre way to apportion “sport” options.


The reliable but boring 2.5-liter four-cylinder 2AR-FE engine.


Rob Siegel


Still, I emailed the seller, verified that there were no rust holes he was aware of and that the A/C worked, got the VIN, and ordered the Carfax. It showed an accident to the right front in 2010, when the car was practically new, but no salvage title. The car had lived in Delaware but came up to Massachusetts in 2017. I was curious enough about this six-speed Camry that I scheduled a Saturday morning appointment.


On the day, I loaded up the E39 with plastic ramps, a Tyvek suit, and an OBD-II scanner, and I drove up to Marblehead—a picturesque little peninsula just north of Boston. I knew I was getting close when the number of driveways with sailboats in them increased exponentially. The seller was an affable young man, very honest about the car’s flaws.


Was my E39 530i meeting its replacement?


Rob Siegel


I started the car and immediately noticed that the “loud exhaust” listed in the ad was gone. When I put it up on ramps, I saw that a flex pipe had been welded between the two cats. Out of curiosity, I asked him what he paid. “About $200,” he said. I was jealous—as I’ve written about the Armada, attempts to find a place that does that kind of work for that kind of price around Newton have come up empty.


I poked around the car, and other than a wart-like fill of a rear bumper dent with un-sanded and unpainted Bondo, the body looked decent. The only undercarriage rust I saw was minor surface oxidation.


This was even uglier than the classic meme-generating bumper-corner “Camry boop.”


Rob Siegel


I plugged in the scanner, and the only code it pulled was the low oxygen sensor voltage code the seller had mentioned in the ad. I cleared it so we could see if it reappeared quickly.


As we were about to go on a test-drive, the seller said that, although he’d had the exhaust repaired, there was a new problem—the right front tire had a puncture, and despite having just re-inflated it, the tire pressure light was on, so it was losing air. I looked and found a nail sticking through the middle of the tread, which was good—a tire shop could fix it. Until that’s done, though, I advised him that our drive should be to an auto parts store to buy a can of Fix-a-Flat, so we didn’t get stranded.


Then, the universe did one of those things that just makes you laugh. I began driving the car, we got maybe a hundred yards, then suddenly heard a noise that sounded like we’d run over a roasting pan and were dragging it. The seller said “What the…” and jumped out of the car and looked under it (we were on a small road with zero traffic). He said “It’s dragging a big long thin piece of aluminum.” I said that this was the exhaust heat shield, it wasn’t a big deal, and we could either yank it out or try to tie it up. We got it stuffed back above the resonator, then carefully drove the car to a parking lot near his workplace where he had access to tools. He drilled a few holes in the shield and zip-tied it to a bracket. I commended him on his Hack Mechanic skills and smiled that he was the one under the car, not me.


The fact that the car I was looking at because it might be nice to have something boring and trouble-free required immediate attention ON THE TEST DRIVE was pretty damn funny.


Rob Siegel


As we inched the four miles to an AutoZone for the Fix-a-Flat, I sussed out the car. Two things struck me immediately. The first was that the clutch was engaging in the top two inches of travel, a likely indication that it was original and probably didn’t have a lot of life in it. My interest in the car at a price anywhere near what he was asking plummeted.


But the more visceral issue was that the six-speed wasn’t remotely enough to overcome the fact that the Camry was so soft and numb that owning it would drive me absolutely crazy. It was like driving a hassock. Maybe a loveseat. As Peter Egan famously wrote in the March 2013 issue of *Road & Track* , “I’ve discovered that a dull car is a lack of joy forever. It weighs on the soul, and you can’t forget for one moment that you aren’t having any fun. You look down the hood, and it’s like having an apartment with an ugly view. You want to close the curtains, but you can’t, because you’re driving.” It was a wake-up call and a reminder: We have these long-term allegiances to cars like my E39 530i because they satisfy what we’re looking for, whether we’ve enumerated the reasons or not.


The seller was a nice guy, and since I already knew I was unlikely to make an offer on the car and had eaten up much of his Saturday morning, I bought him the can of Fix-a-Flat. However, since there was a gas station with an air pump right next to the AutoZone, I told him that, if he thought he was going to get the flat repaired, it was better *not* to shoot in the Fix-a-Flat, since tire shops hate having to deal with it. He elected to simply re-inflate the tire. We did all four (hey, you want to get the most out of that $2 credit card charge for air), but as I was driving back, the front end still didn’t feel quite right. Was it some residual damage from the accident the Carfax listed in 2010? Don’t know, but the uncertainty lowered my interest in the car to zero. But on the plus side, the oxygen sensor code didn’t come back on.


I thanked the seller for his time and his honesty and said that, due both to the likely impending need for a clutch and the car’s being further than expected from what I was used to driving, I was unlikely to make an offer. A few days later he texted me saying that someone else was seriously interested, but wanted to give me one last shot, which I appreciated.


Two days later, it was sold. So someone else also found the ad for the car interesting, but the experience of driving it that revulsed me apparently sealed the deal for them. Vive la différence!


So, that was that. It’s back to things that make sense. You know, 220,000-mile daily-driver BMWs and vintage Lotuses and stuff.


Next month: The Camry SE V-6 manual transmission swap and rear brace removal.


Wait, what?


***
